theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Deriving and Designing RC Oscillators

The numbers 1/(2πRC√6) and 29 come from analysing the three-section high-pass ladder (series C, shunt R) with ordinary circuit laws. Writing α = 1/(ωRC) and solving the ladder from the output back to the input gives the transfer ratio below. Oscillation needs the network output to be exactly 180° from its input, which means the ratio must be a negative real number, so its imaginary part must vanish: 6α − α³ = 0, giving α² = 6 and ω = 1/(RC√6). Substituting α² = 6 into the real part gives 1 − 30 = −29, so the network returns −1/29 of its input and the amplifier must supply a gain of at least 29.

Two variations are worth knowing. If the sections are low-pass (series R, shunt C) the same algebra holds with α replaced by ωRC, so the frequency becomes √6/(2πRC) while the attenuation is still 1/29. If each section is isolated by a buffer, the sections no longer load one another: each simply gives 60°, which happens when ωRC = 1/√3, and each attenuates by cos 60° = 0.5, so the network passes 1/8 and a gain of only 8 is needed. The loading between sections is what makes the unbuffered ladder so lossy.

For the Wien lead-lag network with equal parts, the imaginary term vanishes only when ωRC = 1, which gives f = 1/(2πRC) and β = 1/3. Below this frequency the network leads, above it the network lags, and at every other frequency |β| is less than 1/3, which is what makes the network frequency-selective. With unequal arms (series R_s, C_s; parallel R_p, C_p) the network still has 0° at f = 1/(2π√(R_sC_sR_pC_p)), but its attenuation becomes 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s), so the amplifier gain must rise to match.

Worked example 1: op-amp phase-shift oscillator for 800 Hz
Choose C = 10 nF in each section.
R = 1/(2π f C √6) = 1/(2π × 800 × 10^-8 × 2.449)
  = 8.12 kΩ  ->  nearest standard value 8.2 kΩ
Actual f = 1/(2π × 8200 × 10^-8 × 2.449) ≈ 792 Hz
The inverting amplifier's input resistor is the third R (8.2 kΩ,
returned to the virtual earth), so gain = R_f/R ≥ 29:
R_f ≥ 29 × 8.2 kΩ = 237.8 kΩ  ->  use about 250 kΩ for start-up

Worked example 2: Wien network with unequal capacitors
R_s = R_p = 10 kΩ, C_s = 10 nF, C_p = 20 nF
f = 1/(2π √(R_s C_s R_p C_p))
  = 1/(2π √(10^4 × 10^-8 × 10^4 × 2×10^-8))
  = 1/(2π × 1.414 × 10^-4) ≈ 1.125 kHz
Attenuation = 1/(1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s) = 1/(1 + 1 + 2) = 1/4
Required gain A = 4 = 1 + R_f/R_1  ->  R_f = 3 R_1

The twin-T oscillator uses a notch network made of two T sections in parallel: one T has two series resistors R with a shunt capacitor 2C, the other has two series capacitors C with a shunt resistor R/2. At f = 1/(2πRC) the two paths cancel and the output of the network is zero. Placed in the negative-feedback path of an amplifier, the twin-T removes negative feedback only at the notch frequency, so a modest positive feedback path makes the loop gain exceed unity there and nowhere else, giving a sharply selective audio oscillator.

rows: 3 buffered high-pass RC sections (series C), 60° each

theoryAdd.text: Common mistakes in RC oscillator calculations:
items: Putting √6 in the Wien bridge formula, or leaving it out of the phase-shift formula.
Writing the Wien condition as R_f = 3R_1; the gain is 1 + R_f/R_1 = 3, so R_f = 2R_1.
Using 6 instead of √6, which makes the phase-shift frequency 2.45 times too low.
Forgetting that frequency varies as 1/(RC): doubling both R and C divides f by four.
For a FET or transistor stage, ignoring r_d or R_C loading, which raises the gain actually needed.

theoryAdd.text: Quick checks: with the same R and C, a Wien bridge runs √6 ≈ 2.45 times faster than a phase-shift oscillator. The gain numbers 3 and 29 are independent of the R and C values, so they can be used without any calculation.

questions.questionText: In a three-section RC phase-shift oscillator with identical sections, the phase shift contributed by each RC section at the oscillation frequency is:
questions.explanation: The network must give 180° in total, and three identical sections share it, so each gives 60° (an ideal single section can never reach 90°).

questions.questionText: The amplifier used in an RC phase-shift oscillator must provide a phase shift of:
questions.explanation: The RC network gives 180°, so the amplifier must be inverting and add another 180° to make the loop 360°.

questions.questionText: For an RC phase-shift oscillator with three identical RC sections, the minimum voltage gain of the amplifier is:
questions.explanation: The network attenuates the signal to 1/29 at the oscillation frequency, so |A| ≥ 29 gives |Aβ| ≥ 1.

questions.questionText: The voltage gain of the amplifier in a Wien bridge oscillator must be:
questions.explanation: The lead-lag network passes 1/3 of the output at f0, so a gain of 3 makes the loop gain exactly 1.

questions.questionText: RC oscillators are mainly used to generate sine waves in the:
questions.explanation: RC oscillators work well from a few hertz to about 1 MHz; above that, stray capacitance and amplifier limits favour LC and crystal oscillators.

questions.questionText: The amplifier in a Wien bridge oscillator is a:
questions.explanation: The lead-lag network gives 0° at f0, so the amplifier must also give 0° (non-inverting) for a 360° loop.

questions.questionText: At the oscillation frequency of a Wien bridge oscillator, the phase shift of the lead-lag network is:
questions.explanation: The lead of the series R-C arm exactly cancels the lag of the parallel R-C arm at f = 1/(2πRC), giving 0°.

questions.questionText: At the oscillation frequency, the output of the Wien bridge lead-lag network (with equal R and C) is what fraction of its input?
questions.explanation: With ωRC = 1 the transfer ratio 1/(3 + j(ωRC − 1/(ωRC))) reduces to 1/3.

questions.questionText: RC oscillators are preferred to LC oscillators at low (audio) frequencies mainly because:
options: The inductors needed would be large, heavy and lossy
RC networks have a higher Q than LC tanks
RC oscillators are more stable than crystal oscillators
questions.explanation: At low frequencies f = 1/(2π√(LC)) would demand very large inductors; resistors and capacitors of suitable values are small and cheap.

questions.questionText: The twin-T network used in a twin-T oscillator behaves as a:
options: Notch (band-stop) filter with zero output at f0
Band-pass filter with maximum output at f0
questions.explanation: The two T paths cancel at f0 = 1/(2πRC), so the network output is zero at that frequency and rises on either side: a notch filter.

questions.questionText: In a twin-T oscillator, the twin-T network is connected in:
options: Parallel with the load as a filter
The negative-feedback path, so that negative feedback is minimum at f0
questions.explanation: Because the twin-T rejects f0, negative feedback through it vanishes at f0; a small positive feedback then gives loop gain above 1 only at that frequency.

questions.questionText: A twin-T network uses two series resistors R in one T and two series capacitors C in the other. The shunt elements of the two T sections are:
options: A capacitor C/2 and a resistor 2R
A capacitor C and a resistor R
A capacitor 2C and a resistor R/2
questions.explanation: The R-R T needs a shunt capacitor of 2C and the C-C T needs a shunt resistor of R/2 for a perfect null at f0 = 1/(2πRC).

questions.questionText: A twin-T oscillator uses R = 15 kΩ and C = 10 nF in its twin-T network. The oscillation frequency is approximately:
An RC phase-shift oscillator uses R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 22 nF in each of its three sections. Its frequency of oscillation is approximately:
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2πRC√6) = 1/(2π × 4700 × 22 × 10^-9 × 2.449) ≈ 628 Hz. Leaving out √6 gives 1.54 kHz; dividing by 6 instead of √6 gives 257 Hz.

questions.questionText: An RC phase-shift oscillator must run at 1 kHz with R = 10 kΩ in each section. The capacitance needed in each section is about:
questions.explanation: C = 1/(2πfR√6) = 1/(2π × 1000 × 10^4 × 2.449) ≈ 6.50 nF. Without √6 the result would be 15.9 nF (the Wien value).

questions.questionText: A Wien bridge oscillator has R = 33 kΩ and C = 4.7 nF in both arms of its lead-lag network. Its frequency is approximately:
A Wien bridge oscillator is to run at 5 kHz using R = 3.3 kΩ in both arms. The capacitor value required is about:
questions.explanation: C = 1/(2πfR) = 1/(2π × 5000 × 3300) ≈ 9.65 nF. Omitting 2π gives 60.6 nF; dividing by √6 gives 3.94 nF.

questions.questionText: In an op-amp Wien bridge oscillator, the resistor from the inverting input to ground is R_1 = 4.7 kΩ. The minimum value of the feedback resistor R_f for sustained oscillation is:
questions.explanation: The gain 1 + R_f/R_1 must equal 3, so R_f = 2R_1 = 2 × 4.7 kΩ = 9.4 kΩ. Taking R_f = 3R_1 (14.1 kΩ) would give a gain of 4.

questions.questionText: An op-amp RC phase-shift oscillator uses R = 12 kΩ in each section; the third R also serves as the input resistor of the inverting amplifier. The minimum feedback resistor R_f is:
questions.explanation: The inverting gain R_f/R must be at least 29, so R_f ≥ 29 × 12 kΩ = 348 kΩ.

questions.questionText: The minimum amplifier gain of a three-section RC phase-shift oscillator, expressed in decibels, is about:
questions.explanation: 20 log10(29) = 20 × 1.462 ≈ 29.2 dB. Using 10 log gives 14.6 dB, and 9.54 dB is 20 log10(3), the Wien bridge value.

questions.questionText: An op-amp Wien bridge oscillator has R_f = 18 kΩ and R_1 = 10 kΩ. The amplifier gain and the circuit's behaviour are:
options: Gain 2.8; a steady sine wave is produced
questions.explanation: A = 1 + R_f/R_1 = 1 + 18/10 = 2.8. Since 2.8 × 1/3 = 0.93 is less than 1, the loop gain is below unity and no sustained oscillation occurs.

questions.questionText: A Wien bridge oscillator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 1.5 nF in its lead-lag network, R_f = 25 kΩ and R_1 = 10 kΩ, with no amplitude-stabilising element. The frequency and the nature of the output are:
options: 4.33 kHz; the amplitude grows until the op-amp clips
10.6 kHz; a pure sine wave with no limiting
10.6 kHz; the amplitude grows until the op-amp clips
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2π × 10^4 × 1.5 × 10^-9) ≈ 10.6 kHz. The gain is 1 + 25/10 = 3.5, so the loop gain is 3.5/3 ≈ 1.17 > 1 and the amplitude grows until the op-amp saturates, distorting the sine wave.

questions.questionText: A Wien bridge oscillator and an RC phase-shift oscillator use the same R and C values. The ratio f(Wien)/f(phase-shift) is about:
questions.explanation: f(Wien) = 1/(2πRC) and f(phase-shift) = 1/(2πRC√6), so the ratio is √6 ≈ 2.45.

questions.questionText: If both R and C in the lead-lag network of a Wien bridge oscillator are doubled, the frequency of oscillation becomes:
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2πRC); doubling both R and C multiplies RC by 4, so f falls to one quarter.

questions.questionText: A Wien network has R_s = R_p = 10 kΩ, series capacitor C_s = 10 nF and parallel capacitor C_p = 40 nF. The oscillation frequency and the minimum amplifier gain are:
A Wien network uses equal capacitors but unequal resistors: R_s = 20 kΩ in the series arm and R_p = 5 kΩ in the parallel arm. In the op-amp non-inverting amplifier, the minimum ratio R_f/R_1 is:
questions.explanation: Required gain = 1 + R_s/R_p + C_p/C_s = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, and 1 + R_f/R_1 = 6 gives R_f/R_1 = 5. The value 2 applies only to equal arms.

questions.questionText: A transistor RC phase-shift oscillator has R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF and collector resistor R_C = 5 kΩ. Using f = 1/(2πRC√(6 + 4R_C/R)), its frequency is about:
For a transistor RC phase-shift oscillator the current gain must satisfy h_fe ≥ 23 + 29(R/R_C) + 4(R_C/R). If R_C = R, the minimum h_fe is:
questions.explanation: With R_C/R = 1: h_fe ≥ 23 + 29 + 4 = 56. The value 44.5 is the lowest possible minimum, reached only when R_C/R ≈ 2.7.

questions.questionText: In the transistor RC phase-shift oscillator, h_fe ≥ 23 + 29(R/R_C) + 4(R_C/R). The smallest h_fe that can sustain oscillation, obtained by choosing the best R_C/R, is about:
A FET RC phase-shift oscillator uses a FET with g_m = 4 mS and a very large r_d. The minimum drain resistor R_D is:
questions.explanation: The gain |A| = g_m R_D must be at least 29, so R_D ≥ 29/(4 × 10^-3 S) = 7.25 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A FET RC phase-shift oscillator uses a FET with g_m = 5 mS and r_d = 40 kΩ. The minimum drain resistor R_D, taking r_d into account, is about:
questions.explanation: Need g_m(R_D || r_d) ≥ 29, so R_D || r_d ≥ 29/5 mS = 5.8 kΩ. Then 1/R_D = 1/5.8 kΩ − 1/40 kΩ, giving R_D ≈ 6.78 kΩ. Ignoring r_d gives 5.8 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A Wien bridge oscillator has an output of 6 V peak. The peak voltage fed back by the lead-lag network to the non-inverting input is:
questions.explanation: At f0 the lead-lag network passes 1/3 of the output: 6 V/3 = 2 V, and the amplifier gain of 3 restores it to 6 V.

questions.questionText: An op-amp RC phase-shift oscillator produces an output of 14.5 V peak-to-peak. The peak-to-peak signal at the output of the three-section RC network is:
questions.explanation: The network attenuates by 29, so the signal returned is 14.5/29 = 0.5 V peak-to-peak (and 180° out of phase with the output).

questions.questionText: Which statement about the RC phase-shift oscillator is NOT correct?
options: Its frequency is easily varied over a wide range with a single potentiometer
It needs an amplifier gain of at least 29
Its three RC sections together give 180° of phase shift
questions.explanation: Changing the frequency requires changing all three R or C values together, so the phase-shift oscillator is normally used at a fixed frequency.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the Wien bridge oscillator is correct?
options: It uses both positive feedback and negative feedback
It needs an amplifier gain of at least 29
questions.explanation: The lead-lag network provides positive feedback at f0, while the R_f-R_1 divider provides negative feedback that sets the gain to 3.

questions.questionText: A tungsten lamp is used as R_1 in a Wien bridge oscillator. As the output amplitude increases, the lamp resistance:
options: Increases, which reduces the amplifier gain
Decreases, which increases the amplifier gain
questions.explanation: A tungsten filament has a positive temperature coefficient; more current heats it, R_1 rises and the gain 1 + R_f/R_1 falls, stabilising the amplitude.

questions.questionText: An NTC thermistor is used to stabilise the amplitude of a Wien bridge oscillator. It should be placed in the:
options: Series arm of the lead-lag network
Parallel arm of the lead-lag network
questions.explanation: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as it heats with rising output; in the R_f position this lowers 1 + R_f/R_1 and so reduces the gain. In the R_1 position it would increase the gain and make things worse.

questions.questionText: Two back-to-back diodes are connected across part of the feedback resistor R_f of a Wien bridge oscillator. Their purpose is to:
options: Conduct at large amplitudes, lowering the effective R_f and the gain
questions.explanation: At small amplitude the diodes are off and the gain is a little above 3 for start-up; at large amplitude they conduct, shunt part of R_f and bring the gain back to 3.

questions.questionText: The frequency of a laboratory Wien bridge oscillator is usually varied by:
options: Ganged variable capacitors or resistors in both arms of the lead-lag network
questions.explanation: Both arms must change together to keep equal R and C, so a dual (ganged) capacitor or potentiometer is used; R_f and R_1 only set the gain.

questions.questionText: An RC phase-shift oscillator cannot be built with only two RC sections because:
options: Two sections approach 180° only as their attenuation becomes infinite
Two sections give 360° of phase shift
Two sections can produce only a square wave
questions.explanation: Each RC section gives less than 90°, so two sections reach 180° only in the limit where the output falls to zero; three (or more) sections are needed for a finite gain.

questions.questionText: A phase-shift oscillator uses three identical low-pass RC sections (series R, shunt C) instead of high-pass sections. Its frequency of oscillation is:
questions.explanation: For the low-pass ladder the imaginary part of the transfer ratio vanishes when (ωRC)² = 6, so f = √6/(2πRC); the attenuation is still 1/29.

questions.questionText: A phase-shift oscillator uses three identical RC high-pass sections, each isolated from the next by a unity-gain buffer so there is no loading. At the oscillation frequency, the minimum amplifier gain is:
questions.explanation: Each isolated section must give 60°, and at that frequency its gain is cos 60° = 0.5, so the network passes 0.5³ = 1/8 and the amplifier needs |A| ≥ 8.

questions.questionText: An RC phase-shift oscillator is required to run at 1.2 kHz with C = 10 nF in each section. The resistance needed in each section is about:
A Wien bridge oscillator uses C = 10 nF in both arms and a ganged potentiometer that sets both resistors anywhere from 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ. The frequency range covered is about:
Which oscillator gives the lowest distortion and is the usual choice for a variable-frequency audio test oscillator?
questions.explanation: The Wien bridge, with its gain set by negative feedback and amplitude control, gives a very pure sine wave and is easily tuned with ganged components.

questions.questionText: An RC phase-shift oscillator with identical sections has an amplifier gain of only 25. The circuit will:
options: Oscillate normally with a pure sine wave
Not sustain oscillation, because the loop gain is 25/29, less than 1
questions.explanation: The network passes 1/29 at the only frequency with the correct phase, so the loop gain is 25/29 ≈ 0.86 and any oscillation dies out.

questions.questionText: A twin-T oscillator is to work at 400 Hz with R = 20 kΩ in the series arms of the resistive T. The series capacitor C, the shunt capacitor and the shunt resistor are:
options: C = 19.9 nF, shunt capacitor 9.95 nF, shunt resistor 40 kΩ
C = 8.12 nF, shunt capacitor 16.2 nF, shunt resistor 10 kΩ
C = 19.9 nF, shunt capacitor 39.8 nF, shunt resistor 10 kΩ
C = 19.9 nF, shunt capacitor 39.8 nF, shunt resistor 40 kΩ
questions.explanation: C = 1/(2πf0R) = 1/(2π × 400 × 2 × 10^4) ≈ 19.9 nF. The resistive T has a shunt capacitor 2C = 39.8 nF and the capacitive T a shunt resistor R/2 = 10 kΩ.
